posts.cooked:
I don't think they should have added anything more. This Kickstarter was for the core game, and they set a target for the amount of money the needed to get the game made. Understandably that original target was just to simply get the game made at a basic level that would be adequate for production. I think that's what Kickstarters should be... and people back the project because they want to see that game made as described. Then, stretch goals are set to improve on that game... basically all the things a producer would have wanted to put in the game if they were able to have the money for it. So as pledges come in and you surpass your goal, you begin to hit your stretch goals and get closer and closer to that ideal game. This should all be laid out and planned ahead of time. I believe GTG did that. Once you have reached enough funding to make everything you planned... Well, you simply stop. Mission accomplished. You have raised the money to produce what you need to produce. No need to scramble for additional goals in order to raise more money just to meet those goals you scrambled to create. It's only gonna come off as rushed and probably be I'll received by a lot of people and create negativity that isn't necessary.  I think that's what happened here, GTG told us they got to the end of the planned line for this particular Kickstarter and rushed in to try to appease the horde of stretch goal fiends that Kickstarter has created. I think that was the "mistake" (I put it in quotation marks because I don't really think it was a mistake in the sense that it was the wrong thing to do, but more in the sense that it may have created more headaches than it is worth)

If at the end of a campaign where you have achieved your goal to find the shiniest game you had planned to make, you find yourself with a lot more money than you expected and you want to really thanks all those people who believed in you and your product... throw a little something in for all your backers, and THAT can be an exclusive at that point, because that really is a "thank you".

I don't have a real problem with the concept of Kickstarter exclusives when they are used as a means to entice people to put up the money to get a product made. It's a way of thanking those whose support made the project possible and in essence allowed it to even become available to the people who came later. 
 
However, having said that, I don't believe that's really the case for a lot of Kickstarter campaigns being run these day, and they make little sense to me anymore, except as a money grab (which isn't wrong really, just not something I like to support). These exclusives have gone from "hey, here's a token of appreciation for believing in us and supporting the creation of our product" to "hey, here's a chance for you to buy a badge that says you're cool"... again, don't think this is wrong necessarily, I'm just a little uncomfortable with companies exploiting people's neuroses and insecurities like that.  Whether that actually alienates more people than it entices, I don't know. We'll have to see what happens in the future for companies like CMON (which it hasn't seemed to hurt so far...)

I think it was someone on the DiceTower, or maybe Giant Fire-Breathing Robot, who said the best way to do KS exclusives are "time limited" - your exclusivity is a period of 6 months/1 year from the retail launch of the product. It's less valuable than true exclusives, but still gives people something for backing the product without permanently denying the wider audience.

In terms of internet retail being cheaper than bricks and mortar, it's not the case that the internet sells them at a loss, as generally their operating costs are lower. You don't simple pay for a game - you pay the wholesale cost of the game, plus the costs of storing and shipping the stock, the staff wages (and benefits), the costs of the store and other things, plus the profit margin. Internet retailers can make much more financially efficient use of their space since they don't have to worry about presentation (and have fewer staff in relation to how much stock they carry). I suspect games companies could undercut internet retailers selling directly, but doing so would undermine the retail/distribution channels, so they'll generally sell the game at MSRP and add exclusive extras (promo cards etc), and retailers take on some of the storage burden btu can discount

Back on to Sentinels - I was underwhelmed by the first game-play vid. It felt like a collection of people rolling dice. The second one (Baron Blade scenario) was better, it gave a better feel for how it plays, though it would be nice to maybe edit some graphics in showing a power card or two in detail, and maybe cutting away in to someone's though process whilst making a turn ("Well, I switch this power out because..."). That's moved me towards backing the project. One thing I still have reservations about is the use of tokens for the characters (which still seems to be the case in the latest update) - you can see in the second video someone hit some effects tokens reaching to move their character. Stand-up cardboard pieces would look better, and be more user friendly (I suspect they might also help visually impaired gamers if all characters/targets distinguish themselves like that)

Regarding stretch goals and the new add-on pack, I think something that too many KS backers obsess on is free-stuff, rather than better stuff! I kept an eye on the KS Campaign for a rival company's worker placement game, and they had some goals that added more things in, eventually including an expansion (available for a higher pledge level), but quite a few goals were things like replacing wooden pawns with plastic figures and replacing cardboard coins with plastic, once they hit a point where economies of scale let them do so. This campaign has added stuff, eventually completing the planned versions (which I said to someone on FaceBook that it's a strength and weakness of GtG - they bind the games brilliantly to story, but the story also constrains what they can do with releases). I dislike the idea of poster maps - my brother and I had Marvel Superheroes from TSR back in the day which used paper maps and they can only survive so much folding and unfolding, so I wonder if a stretch goal could be having them in a board format somewhere along the line? Or maybe have the poster maps as a KS 'exclusive', with the retail version printed on to the same material as the playmat for SotM?

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
Exclusives, big reward deals and such might get you a big number on your kickstarter, but what it won't do is give you a predictor for future non-kickstarter success.

This Kickstarter is not an attempt to get enough capitol to make Sentinels Tactics, it is just the best method for >G to test the market for the game.

If it does well on Kickstarter because they gave some really cool SotM crossover rewards or a bunch of exclusives then they didn't get a good look at the future of the game.

This Kickstarter is going to show them the viability of different strategies and products, like whether painted Mini's would be worth making a product they sell with a later expansion, or if poster or hex block maps are a better way to do their maps., as well as give them an idea of how big a market there is for the game.  It isn't going to tell them how many people love exclusives, or how many people will buy a new game to get SotM promos.

This isn't a small company willing to do anything to get you to buy their game so that word gets out and the game spreads.  >G has been there, they aren't there anymore.  They aren't going to make a big investment with little profit now.  This is a very different style of Kickstarter from what people the Kickstarter crowd likes to see, but it is a great use of the platform.

Aerial Photography maps are awesome, but generally expensive because you have to alter them quite a bit to make the elevation changes fit into hexes, or it ends up looking like you forced a hex grid onto something that doesn't fit.

There are several people who do it for the steampunk Zepellin game and Battletech, or at least did 2 years ago, I can't find their stuff now.

 

There are programs like Hexographer that let you make your own, but not with photos.

If the game gets big enough someone will jump on it and sell some cool maps like that on Ebay.

posts.name: Spiff
posts.cooked:
Bas:

Curious with the possibilities to make a custom environment tiles, here is a quick attempt featuring the Eiffel tower.

Love it.

I've already made a full set of Insula Primalis tiles and about half a set of Megalopolis tiles, back when all we got for playtesting were tiles with blocks of color on them.  I used basic Photoshopping skills, plus some 3D models from Google's Sketchup (the app that lets anyone make 3D models for their maps) and some Dundjinni top-down art assets for things like trees and cars.  It's not that hard, and I expect to see a whole raft of custom tiles from fans once the game comes out.
